name: Odd number of divisors means a square
formula: d(n) \text{ is odd} \iff n \text{ is a perfect square}
whenToUse: Toggling problems (lockers, lights, switches) or any question about numbers with an odd number of divisors.
example: $100$ lockers start closed and locker $k$ is toggled once for each divisor of $k$. The open ones at the end are those toggled an odd number of times, the perfect squares $1, 4, \ldots, 100$: ten lockers.
pitfall: Numbers with exactly $3$ divisors are a stricter set: squares of primes, like $4$, $9$, $25$.
derivation: Divisors pair up as $d$ and $\frac{n}{d}$. The only divisor that can pair with itself is $\sqrt{n}$, so the count is odd exactly when $\sqrt{n}$ is an integer.
